title: Master Class | Center Game | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: If it ain't broke — we roll out the Danish/Center Game again, opening with d4 against the king-pawn.
He meets it with knight f6, an uncommon and not-great try that counterattacks our e4-pawn — but that knight is about to go wandering into trouble in my position.
We snap off e5 first, opening lines.

He grabs on e4. Here's the key idea: a knight can be centralized and still deeply vulnerable if no pawns or pieces support it — that's exactly this knight. Don't be reactive: Qe2 lets it drop to c5 and boxes in your bishop, and f3 walks into the Qh4+ then Nxg3 pattern.
teaches: A centralized knight without support is a target, not a strength
Don\u2019t react to a loose knight — find the opponent\u2019s other weaknesses

moves.spoken: Instead we ignore the knight and hit the real weak spot: f7. The bishop to c4 pressures f7 and, since the knight is undefended, sets up forks that hit both at once.
teaches: Target f7 early; combine pressure on it with the loose knight

moves.spoken: The queen to h4 — a delayed response that forks the knight and swings at the king together. Careful though: the tempting g3 loses, because the queen x-rays our own c4-bishop, so after g3 Nxg3 the queen slides over and wins the undefended bishop.
teaches: Watch for a discovered attack when your queen and a loose bishop share a line

moves.spoken: We reposition the queen to f3, keeping the heat on f7 — a near-mate threat that deters his discoveries and buys us time. When you have a strong card, hold it and play it when it hits hardest.
teaches: Exercise restraint — play your strong move when it lands with most force
plans: Bring the queen into the queenside pressure next

moves.spoken: On the recap: the point of the bishop to c4 is that it isn't just development — it sets up Qd5 and Qf3. Hold your good moves close and they hit far harder than if you rush them.
teaches: Develop with a follow-up threat in mind
